title: Is Renting Getting Worse? The Data Behind the Squeeze

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Renting has become an increasingly heavy burden for the typical household. The cost of having a place to call home has quietly reached a historic peak.

segments.label: scene 2 (counter)
segments.text: If we look back to January 1990, residential rent prices have surged by 232%.

segments.label: scene 3 (line)
segments.text: In fact, today's rent index sits at 3.3 times what it was at the start of that decade.

segments.label: scene 4 (statement)
segments.text: This shift isn't just about the long term; it's a persistent, compounding pressure.

segments.label: scene 5 (counter)
segments.text: Even over the last five years, rent has climbed by 33%.

segments.label: scene 6 (heatmap)
segments.text: And in just the past year alone, prices ticked up another 2.8%.

segments.label: scene 7 (multiline)
segments.text: The math is clear: the path of rent prices is moving consistently upward, outpacing many other household concerns.

segments.label: scene 8 (statement)
segments.text: To understand why rent feels heavier, we must look at the long-term trend. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, costs have compounded relentlessly.

segments.label: scene 9 (line)
segments.text: If we look back to January 1995, rent prices have climbed 189% by today. This marks a steady, decades-long rise in what tenants pay.

segments.label: scene 10 (line)
segments.text: By the turn of the millennium in January 2000, that cumulative growth sits at 149%. The climb never seems to plateau.

segments.label: scene 11 (line)
segments.text: Looking at January 2005, the increase since then is 110%. Each interval consistently shows this mounting pressure.

segments.label: scene 12 (multiline)
segments.text: Even by January 2010, after the housing crisis, rent prices have still grown 81% against today's levels.

segments.label: scene 13 (bars)
segments.text: Moving to January 2015, we see a 60% jump since that point. The data reveals a clear, persistent upward trajectory.

segments.label: scene 14 (heatmap)
segments.text: Every decade brings higher thresholds. Rent isn't just rising; it is compounding across every major benchmark we analyze.

segments.label: scene 15 (line)
segments.text: To understand this squeeze, we look at vacancy rates. These numbers reveal how much breathing room exists in the rental market.

segments.label: scene 16 (counter)
segments.text: In October 2021, availability hit a historic low of 5.6%. Apartments vanished from the market almost instantly.

segments.label: scene 17 (statement)
segments.text: Low vacancy acts as a pressure cooker for prices. When supply drops, competition among renters inevitably intensifies.

segments.label: scene 18 (counter)
segments.text: By July 2026, the vacancy rate had crept back up to 7.6%. This is barely a 1% change from 1990 levels.

segments.label: scene 19 (compare)
segments.text: Even with this slight easing, the market remains tight compared to the 11.1% peak seen in 2009.

segments.label: scene 20 (counter)
segments.text: This scarcity has lasting effects. Since January 2020, vacancy rates have risen 15%, reflecting a very different landscape.

segments.label: scene 21 (multiline)
segments.text: The math is simple: fewer available units mean landlords hold the leverage. Rent becomes a buyer's market for the owner.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Why has renting become such a volatile game? To understand, we have to look back at the 2008 financial crisis.

segments.label: scene 23 (counter)
segments.text: Back in July 2009, the market was flooded with vacancies, hitting a peak of 11.1%.

segments.label: scene 24 (line)
segments.text: Developers essentially stopped building for years. The ripple effect of that slowdown created a massive supply deficit.

segments.label: scene 25 (counter)
segments.text: Then, the pandemic hit. In January 2020, vacancy rates were already tight at 6.6%.

segments.label: scene 26 (line)
segments.text: Suddenly, everyone scrambled for space, pushing vacancy rates down to 5.6% by October 2021.

segments.label: scene 27 (kpi)
segments.text: Recent apartment building booms have finally begun to help, as vacancy rates rose 7% over the last year.

segments.label: scene 28 (compare)
segments.text: Even with this progress, we are still 32% lower than the vacancy highs we saw in 2009.

segments.label: scene 29 (statement)
segments.text: But while rents surged, what happened to our paychecks? That is the real test of affordability.

segments.label: scene 30 (counter)
segments.text: In January 1990, the median household income was $67,050. By January 2025, it reached $87,460.

segments.label: scene 31 (counter)
segments.text: That is a total growth of 30% since 1990. It is a modest gain for the average family.

segments.label: scene 32 (line)
segments.text: Compare that 30% wage growth to the 232% surge in rent over the exact same period.

segments.label: scene 33 (statement)
segments.text: Rent has been climbing much faster than income. The burden on household budgets has expanded significantly.

segments.label: scene 34 (multiline)
segments.text: Since January 2020, inflation-adjusted median household income has grown 5%, while rent prices have climbed 33%.

segments.label: scene 35 (line)
segments.text: This divergence is why renting feels increasingly unaffordable. Rent is taking a larger slice of the pie.

segments.label: scene 36 (statement)
segments.text: So, where does that leave the average renter today? The data shows a persistent, heavy drag on household finances.

segments.label: scene 37 (kpi)
segments.text: In the last year alone, median household income grew by 2.6%. It's a positive step, but look at how it compares to rent.

segments.label: scene 38 (line)
segments.text: Rent prices have outpaced those gains, climbing 2.8% over that same recent twelve-month window.

segments.label: scene 39 (line)
segments.text: Looking at the period since January 2025, rent is up 5%. The momentum hasn't broken yet.

segments.label: scene 40 (multiline)
segments.text: Since 1995, rent has surged by 189%, outpacing income growth significantly.

segments.label: scene 41 (line)
segments.text: Ultimately, rent is consuming more of our earnings than ever. It's a structural imbalance that isn't correcting itself.

segments.label: scene 42 (line)
segments.text: Have you seen rent prices flatten out in your own neighborhood? Tell us in the comments. Subscribe for more data stories.
